concordance.note: Different objects under the same headline. Coen measures advertiser billings bottom-up at list (rate-card) prices across eleven media including business papers and a ~20%-of-total 'miscellaneous' bucket. MAGNA's MG8 measures media-supplier revenue top-down across eight media with no miscellaneous and no business papers. 1980 is the only year both compilers publish: MCE $53,570m vs MG8 $41,021m. Re

Both carry a line called 'internet'. Coen's is an advertiser-billings estimate that the dataset's own curator calls a serious underestimate from 2004; IAB/PwC's is a seller-reported revenue survey. The gap widens every year of the overlap. Any chart that stacks Coen's media partition must keep Coen's internet line, or the partition stops summing to Coen's total.

Category rename with a scope change. 'Billboards' is a partition member 1935-1999; 'Out of Home' replaces it from 1999 (published for both bases in 1999) and carries transit, street furniture, place-based and other formats. Reading the two as one series manufactures a 177% jump in 2000.

One published 'Television' line becomes two published lines, 'Broadcast TV' and 'Cable', in 1990. Coen's own scheme-2 sub-categories let the split be pushed back to 1980 exactly (they sum to the Television line); before 1980 no cable line exists at all. This dataset carries the 1980-1989 broadcast/cable pair as constructed grade-C points.

The same year has different values in different vintages of the same series. Against the Printers'-Ink-lineage figures printed in Historical Statistics (T 444), the Coen-2000 vintage revised the 1920s down by 15-18%; 1932-1945 moves by under 2%; and the 1999 total was revised UP 3.3% between the 2000 and 2003 vintages. The 1920s revision is large enough to change the ad/GDP story for that decade.

By-medium detail does not exist before 1935. For 1919-1934 the published partition is three lines: newspapers, other periodicals, and 'other' -- and the CS Ad Dataset's finer categories for those years are part Coen, part other sources, part the curator's own estimates. Radio's own line begins in 1935, thirteen years after commercial radio advertising began.

Partition members appear and disappear mid-series. Yellow Pages appears in 1980 at $2,900m with no restatement of earlier years (it was previously inside miscellaneous, which drops by a comparable amount in the same year). Farm Publications ($212m) and the magazine sub-categories are dropped after 1989. A stacked chart must show these as entries and exits, not as growth and collapse.

Coen's newspaper line IS the NAA publisher survey, unadjusted, for 1950-1989 (identical to the dollar in 36 of 40 years). From 1990 Coen adjusts it: he runs up to 0.86% ABOVE NAA in the mid-to-late 1990s and about 0.2% below it in the 2000s. The two are therefore not independent -- NAA cannot validate Coen's newspaper line, it only supplies the national / retail / classified split Coen does not pu

The Census enumerates what publishers RECEIVED; Coen estimates what advertisers SPENT. The wedge is agency commission, production and the difference between list and net. The CS Ad Dataset applies a 1.5187 factor to Census newspaper receipts to build its pre-1935 newspaper estimates, so for those years the Coen newspaper line is a scaled Census figure rather than an independent measurement.

Advertiser billings (Coen) against the advertising deduction on corporate tax returns (IRS). Silk & Berndt report r = 0.998 between them over 1960-2007. In the three overlap years available here Coen runs 0.8% to 7.1% above IRS. IRS is used only as a cross-check and is never stitched.

After the Coen series ends the two rails diverge hard and in one direction: the IRS deduction keeps growing faster than media-owner revenue. In 2022 the IRS advertising deduction is $473bn against a MAGNA US media-owner revenue of about $325bn -- a 31% gap, well past the 15% tolerance. This is a measurement finding, not an error: the tax line absorbs promotion, agency and martech spend that never

Treat MAGNA's digital line as the IAB series carried through, not as an independent estimate: adding them, or using one to check the other, double-counts.

IAB restates. This dataset uses one vintage throughout -- the FY2025 report's historical table -- so that year-on-year changes are not vintage artefacts. Earlier vintages print 2015 as $59,550m and 2016 as $72,521m (FY2015 edition of April 2016, FY2016 edition of April 2017 and FY2017 edition of May 2018 all agree); the FY2025 vintage prints $59,551m and $72,640m. The largest restatement inside th

Two retrospective vintages of the pre-1919 record disagree systematically: the Printers' Ink figures in HSUS T 444 run 9-20% above Coen's 1999 revision of the same years, with no consistent gradient (1904 +9.5%, 1909 +14.2%, 1917 +17.9%, 1900 +20.4%). Points here take the midpoint with a CI spanning both. Before 1867 there is no estimate of any kind, so 1840-1866 is a hole, not a low number.
The bridge ribbon is the Coen ribbon restated onto MAGNA's basis. It is derived FROM coen_mce and is not an independent measurement: never sum the two, never treat their agreement as corroboration.

At 1980 the bridge reproduces MAGNA's published MG8 value by construction (the wedge is calibrated there), so 1980 is an identity, not a test. The bridge's only out-of-sample test is 2007, against GroupM's independently published US measured-media total.

The NAA table does not add up in two of its 61 years: national + retail + classified overshoots the printed print total by $14m in 1956 and falls $30m short in 1957, and the printed year-on-year percentages for those rows are inconsistent with the printed dollars. Four further years (1991, 1996, 2005, 2006) differ by $1m from rounding. The published values are carried unaltered and the residual is

NAA's newspaper online revenue is a subset of the IAB internet total, and from 2003 NAA reports print and online separately. Adding NAA's combined total to the IAB internet line double-counts newspaper digital revenue -- $3,166m of it in 2007.

thread1_measurement.name: The Middlemen
thread1_measurement.summary: The counted thing was circulation, and for most of the era nobody counted it honestly. Publishers stated their own figures, and advertisers had no way to test them, which is why the rate card was unenforceable. The first counting institution was commercial: George P. Rowell's American Newspaper Directory (1869) listed 5,778 US papers with Rowell's own estimated circulations, and N. W. Ayer's American Newspaper Annual followed in 1880. Advertisers then tried to police publishers themselves through the Association of American Advertisers, which folded in 1913. Government moved next: the Newspaper Publicity Act of 24 August 1912 made the cheap second-class mailing rate conditional on filing a s

thread1_measurement.name: Sponsorship
thread1_measurement.summary: Broadcasting had no circulation to audit, so the era had to invent one, and the whole history turns on who paid the counter. The Cooperative Analysis of Broadcasting began field work in March 1930 with the Association of National Advertisers' endorsement, funded by advertisers at $70 a month, and deliberately excluded the networks as subscribers until 1937 - buyers were counting the sellers' goods. Its method was 24-hour telephone recall, and its central defect was the telephone itself: by 1934-35, 96 percent of telephone subscribers owned radios but only 31 percent of American families had telephones, so the sample over-represented the well-off. thread1_measurement.name: The Spot Market
thread1_measurement.summary: The spot market could not exist without a currency, and in this era the currency was Nielsen. Nielsen bought C. E. Hooper's national radio and television ratings business in March 1950 and thereafter faced no serious national competitor; Arbitron (American Research Bureau) competed locally. The technology was two-layered and the layering matters: a small meter panel - the Audimeter, about 1,100-1,200 households - measured whether a set was on and what it was tuned to, and separate diary panels supplied the age and sex breaks that turned households into demographics. The Nielsen Station Index brought diary measurement to local markets from 1954. In September 1973 the Storage Instantaneous Aud

thread1_measurement.name: Segmentation
thread1_measurement.summary: Every price in this market rested on somebody's count, and in 1987 the count changed. Nielsen replaced diaries and household set meters with people meters as the national currency for the 1987-88 season, and measured prime-time viewing fell roughly 10% overnight; CBS and ABC each lost 13%, NBC 4%, and the Saturday-morning children's audience fell by 20% to 50% against about $150M of network children's advertising. The networks owed make-goods in scatter time worth more than the upfront time they had sold, and they attacked the panel's composition - 33% of people-meter homes had pay cable against 26% of the population. Nothing about the audience had changed; only the instrument had. On the di

thread1_measurement.name: The Impression
thread1_measurement.summary: This is the first era in which the seller counted the audience with its own instrument and the buyer had no third-party audit to appeal to. The counting technology was the ad server: DoubleClick's DART delivered 621 billion ads worldwide in 2000 and its log was the invoice. Two rival counting institutions grew up beside it — server-side log auditors (I/PRO, NetCount, ABC Interactive) and user-panel meters (Media Metrix, RelevantKnowledge, then Nielsen//NetRatings from 1998) — and they disagreed, because proxy caching hid impressions from server logs while panels missed work and school access. thread1_measurement.name: The Auction
thread1_measurement.summary: This is the era in which the seller became the auditor. Every price in the search market was set from a count that the seller alone produced: Google recorded the impression, ran the auction, decided which click was valid, and billed against its own log. No third party audited any of it in period — the IAB's Click Measurement Working Group only convened in late 2005 and its guidelines were not published until 2009, and there was no Media Rating Council accreditation of search click counting during the era. thread1_measurement.name: The Machine Market
thread1_measurement.summary: Era 7 is where the century-old rule that a third party counts the audience finally broke. From ABC in 1914 to MRC accreditation after 1964, the market's discipline was that the buyer could audit someone other than the seller. In this era the same company sold the inventory, ran the auction, counted the impressions and attributed the conversions - and the failures were exactly what that arrangement predicts.
